opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most important questions right now, and honestly I don't think anyone has a complete answer yet. But I can share how I think about it.

To me, the key shift is from a world where the model is trained once and then frozen, to a world where the model keeps learning from its own experience while it's being used. Today most of the improvement still comes from humans: we collect data, design rewards, run a training cycle, and release a new version. The agent itself doesn't really accumulate anything from doing the task. Every new conversation is a bit like waking up with amnesia.

So what would continuous learning actually require? I'd say a few things.

First, the agent needs a good sense of what it's trying to achieve, a kind of internal or environmental reward, rather than relying entirely on a human to label every outcome. In domains like math or coding you can verify results, which is why progress there has been so fast. The harder part is extending that to messier real-world tasks where success is ambiguous.

Second, it needs a way to keep its experience. That could be memory or context that persists across tasks, or it could eventually be updating its own weights. I think in the near term a lot of this will look like memory and context engineering: the agent writes down what worked, what didn't, what the user prefers. Over time that line between "memory" and "learning" will probably blur.

Third, and this is something I care a lot about, the environment matters as much as the model. People talk a lot about the model getting smarter, but the agent can only learn from the experiences it's exposed to. If you put it in rich, real environments with real feedback, real users, real tools, real consequences, it can learn things you could never put into a static dataset. So in some sense the question of self-improvement is really a question of what tasks and environments we let agents operate in.

And I think there's a utility question too. In the first half of AI, we focused on building better methods and beating benchmarks. Now I think we're in a phase where the question is: what's actually useful, and how do we evaluate it? Self-improvement only matters if it's improving toward something people actually value. So defining the right evaluation, the right notion of progress, might end up being more important than any specific algorithm.

My guess is it won't be one dramatic moment where a model suddenly starts improving itself. It'll be gradual: agents with better memory, then agents that adapt to individual users, then agents that learn across many users and tasks, and eventually the training loop and the deployment loop kind of merge into one. That's the direction I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: The response identifies persistent memory or context and eventual weight updates as distinct possible ways an agent could retain experience and improve.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key is to separate two things that people often lump together: the model learning in the moment, and the model learning across moments.

Right now, most of what we call "learning" happens in training. You run RL, the weights update, you ship a checkpoint, and then the model is basically frozen. At deployment time it can use context, it can use tools, it can take notes in a scratchpad or a file system, but nothing it experiences actually changes the model. So the agent you talk to on Monday is the same agent on Friday, no matter how many mistakes it made in between.

I think the first real step toward self-improvement isn't anything exotic. It's just closing that loop. An agent goes out, does a long task, gets some signal about whether it worked, and that experience flows back into training. The reason this hasn't happened at scale is not that it's conceptually hard. It's that the signal is messy. In a game, or in math, or in coding with unit tests, you have a clean reward. In the real world, success is often delayed, partial, or defined by a human who may not even be paying attention. So a lot of the work is actually about environments and evaluation, not about new algorithms. If you can define what "good" means for a task, the RL machinery we already have will find its way there.

The second step, which I find more interesting, is when the agent starts shaping its own learning. Choosing what to practice, generating its own problems, building its own tools, deciding which experiences are worth keeping. This is where the research on agents and the research on training really converge. An agent that can write code, run experiments, and read results is, in principle, an agent that can run its own training loop. Humans would still set the objective, but the model would own more and more of the process underneath.

I'd push back a little on the romantic version of this, though. People imagine one model sitting in a room recursively rewriting itself. I think it'll look much more like a system: many agents, lots of tool use, long memory, and a huge amount of compute spent on verification. Most of the gains will come from the boring parts, like better feedback, better task distributions, and better infrastructure for running millions of trajectories, rather than from some single insight.

And the bottleneck, honestly, is us. The models are already good enough that they're limited less by their own ability and more by whether we can tell them clearly what we want and whether we can check what they did. So when I think about autonomous learning, I think the real question is not "can the model improve itself." It's "can we build the environments and the evaluation where improving itself actually means improving at things we care about."

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes updating model weights through training from using deployment-time context, notes, or long memory, which it says do not change the model itself.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to close the loop between acting, getting feedback, and learning. An agent can already try something, observe what happens, and adjust its next action. But that is different from continuously improving: if it encounters the same problem tomorrow and repeats the same mistake, the learning hasn’t really persisted.

There are several ways to make it persist. The agent can save useful experiences in memory, improve its tools or procedures, or use those experiences to update the underlying model. I don’t think every new experience needs to become a weight update. Part of the challenge is deciding what should be remembered for a particular task and what should become a general capability.

The hardest part, in my view, is the feedback. In coding, you can run a test. In mathematics, you might verify a proof. In more open-ended work, it is much harder to know whether an action was actually good. If the model simply judges its own outputs and trains on the ones it likes, it can reinforce its mistakes. Autonomous learning needs some grounding outside that loop.

So I would expect progress first in environments where agents can try many things and reliably measure the results. Then the question becomes whether they can turn those experiences into improvements that transfer to new tasks. Generating more experience is one thing; learning the right lesson from it is another.

r001.rationale: It identifies saving experiences in memory and updating the underlying model as distinct ways to make learning persist, and notes that not every experience needs a weight update.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to close the loop between acting, getting feedback, and learning. Today, a model can complete a task, but the experience often disappears when the conversation ends. A continuously learning agent would need to turn that experience into something that improves its future behavior.

There are different levels to this. An agent can first improve by remembering useful information, developing better tools, or changing its strategy. That doesn’t necessarily require updating the model’s parameters. Then, over time, you could use those experiences to train the underlying model. So you might have a fast loop of adaptation through memory and a slower loop of improvement through training.

The difficult part is deciding what to learn from. In coding, you can run tests, although passing the tests doesn’t always mean the solution is correct. In more open-ended tasks, the feedback is much less clear. If an agent simply treats its own judgment as ground truth, it can reinforce its mistakes. So autonomous learning needs reliable feedback from the environment, and sometimes from people.

I also think choosing what to try is important. An agent needs to explore tasks that teach it something, rather than repeatedly doing things it already knows how to do. My guess is that we’ll first see this work well in environments where actions are relatively cheap and outcomes are verifiable. The bigger question is how to carry those improvements into broader settings without losing earlier capabilities or learning the wrong lessons.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes improvement through remembering useful information without changing model parameters from later training of the underlying model.
